lead: Three days after Pentecost our Church remembers, by an old tradition, the first Holy Qurbono offered by Mar Yaqob Shleeha, James the brother of the Lord and first bishop of Jerusalem. Both readings take us back to the night when it all began. Paul hands on to the Corinthians what he himself received: the Lord Jesus took bread and the cup and said, “Do this in remembrance of me.” Luke shows the same night from inside the upper room, where Jesus says, “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” The key words are hand on, remembrance and covenant.

r.h: What I received from the Lord
set: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus (16:8), around AD 53–55. The church in Corinth was gifted but divided, and the divisions showed even at the Lord's Supper. When they gathered, some went ahead with their own meal while others, the poor, went hungry (11:20–22). Paul does not answer first with a new rule. He reminds them what the Supper is.

These four verses are the oldest written account of the Last Supper that we have, older than the Gospels in their written form. Paul had taught it to the Corinthians when he founded their church, around AD 50, and he says that it came to him as a tradition from the Lord himself.
str: v. 23a: the chain of tradition: received from the Lord, handed on to you.
vv. 23b–24: the night of betrayal; the bread, the thanksgiving, “This is my body”.
v. 25: the cup after supper: the new covenant in my blood.
v. 26: Paul's comment: every Supper proclaims the Lord's death until he comes.
¶ In the verses that follow Paul draws the lesson: whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup in an unworthy manner will be answerable for the body and blood of the Lord (11:27–29).
kw: The pair of words used for passing on a sacred teaching from teacher to disciple. Paul uses the same pair in 15:3 for the Gospel of the Resurrection. The Eucharist reached Corinth as a gift handed on, not as something the community made up. There is a play on words too: the night when Jesus “was betrayed” uses the same verb. On the night he was handed over, he handed himself over for us.

More than a memory in the mind. In the Bible, to remember before God makes the saving event present. Israel kept the Passover as “a day of remembrance” (Exodus 12:14), and each generation was to tell what the Lord had done for it.
The word used for preaching the Gospel. The Supper itself is a proclamation: it announces the Lord's death as the source of life, and it looks forward to his coming.
vv: the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread,
Paul names the night, not only the meal. The Eucharist is bound to the Passion. It comes from the hour when one disciple handed Jesus over and Jesus gave himself up for all.
“This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

“For you” gives the meaning of the gift: a body given up on behalf of others. Among the four accounts of the Supper, only Paul and Luke keep the command “Do this”, which the Church has always understood as given to the apostles and to those who follow them in their ministry.
This cup is the new covenant in my blood.

Jeremiah promised a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34). At Sinai Moses sprinkled the people with “the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8). Jesus joins the two: the covenant is new, and it is sealed in his own blood.
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
The Supper looks two ways: back to the Cross and forward to the Lord's return. The first Christians prayed in Aramaic, Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!” (16:22).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Eucharist is the memorial of Christ's Passover. In the liturgy this memorial is not only the recalling of past events: the sacrifice that Christ offered once for all on the Cross remains ever present (CCC 1362–1364). The Catechism points to this passage for the Lord's command to repeat his words and actions “until he comes” (CCC 1341). With the Council of Trent it teaches that at the Last Supper Christ instituted the Eucharist and made his apostles priests of the New Testament (CCC 1337). Paul's own concern is also the Church's: the Body of Christ received at the altar cannot be separated from his body the community, and above all from its poorest members. The Eucharist commits us to the poor (CCC 1397).

r.h: I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you
set: Luke places the Supper at the hour of the Passover meal (22:7–13). Jesus has sent Peter and John to prepare it in a large upper room. Luke's account is the longest of the four, because after the meal Jesus goes on speaking with the apostles at the table (22:21–38).

Luke's words over the bread and the cup are very close to Paul's: both have “for you”, “Do this in remembrance of me” and “the new covenant in my blood”. Scholars commonly note that Luke and Paul share one form of the tradition, and Mark and Matthew another. Luke is named as Paul's companion in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24.
str: v. 14: the hour comes; Jesus takes his place with the apostles.
vv. 15–16: his great desire, and the Passover fulfilled in the kingdom of God.
vv. 17–18: a first cup, shared among them.
v. 19: the bread: my body given for you.
v. 20: the cup after supper: the new covenant in my blood, poured out for you.
kw: Literally “with desire I have desired”. The Greek copies a Hebrew way of speaking that doubles a word to make it strong. It shows the heart of Jesus as he goes to his Passion: he does not only accept this meal, he has longed for it.

The feast of Israel's deliverance from Egypt (Exodus 12). Jesus will not eat it again “until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God”. The old feast is not thrown aside; it reaches its fulfilment in him. Paul calls Christ “our paschal lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7).
A word of sacrifice, used of blood poured out at the altar. The Greek is in the present tense: the offering of the Cross is already present at the table.
vv: When the hour came, he took his place at the table, and the apostles with him.
Luke gives the Supper a solemn beginning. The word “apostles”, those who are sent, reminds us that this meal is given to men who will be sent out.
I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer;
Only Luke records this saying. Before we desire the Eucharist, Christ has desired to give himself to us.
“This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

Textual note: a few ancient witnesses, chiefly one Greek manuscript (Codex Bezae) and some Old Latin copies, stop after “This is my body”. Almost all manuscripts have the longer text, and the NRSV and other modern editions print it, as the Church's lectionary does.
This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.

Luke mentions two cups (vv. 17 and 20). The Passover meal, as later Jewish sources describe it, had several cups of wine. Many scholars think the first cup belongs to the Passover rite, and the second, “after supper”, is the cup of the new covenant.
ch: The Church reads this account as the institution of the Eucharist and of the priesthood that serves it. The Catechism says that by celebrating the Last Supper with his apostles in the course of the Passover meal, Jesus gave the Jewish Passover its definitive meaning (CCC 1340). St Ignatius of Antioch, whom our Church honours as Mar Ignatius Noorono, wrote that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins and which the Father raised up (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 7, in substance). The Church takes the Lord at his word, “This is my body”: under the signs of bread and wine Christ is truly, really and substantially present (CCC 1374).

qa: James “the Lord's brother” (Galatians 1:19), who led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; 21:18). He is not James the son of Zebedee, whose death by the sword is told in Acts 12:2 and whom our Church honoured on 30 April. The Latin tradition has usually identified the brother of the Lord with the apostle James the son of Alphaeus; Eastern traditions often keep them apart. The question has never been settled with certainty. “Brother” in the Bible can mean a close relative, and the Church holds that Mary remained ever virgin (CCC 500).
Did Mar Yaqob write the Anaphora that bears his name?

The Anaphora of St James carries his name because it comes from the Church of Jerusalem, where he was the first bishop. Many scholars think its present text took shape in Jerusalem in the fourth century, from older roots, and was then carried to Antioch and beyond. The name honours its source: the church that first devoted itself to “the breaking of bread and the prayers” after Pentecost (Acts 2:42).
rite: Today our Church keeps the memory of the first Holy Qurbono offered by Mar Yaqob, the brother of the Lord. In the West Syriac tradition his name stands first among the anaphoras: the Anaphora of St James is honoured as the chief one, after whose pattern many others were composed. When the priest repeats the words of the Lord over the bread and the cup and the people answer “Amen”, we stand in the chain that Paul describes: what was received from the Lord is handed on. This week after Pentecost also reminds us that the Spirit who came upon the apostles is the same Spirit called down upon the gifts at every Holy Qurbono.
study: Paul says he handed on what he had received. Who handed on the faith of the Holy Qurbono to me, and to whom am I handing it on?
Jesus “eagerly desired” to eat this Passover with his apostles. How can I prepare to meet that desire next Sunday?
Paul links the Lord's Supper with care for the poor of the community. Who goes hungry near my parish table?
